4.3 — Chase: The Aggro Radius

Patrol is calm. One trigger turns a guard into a hunter — and you built that trigger's answer in 3.1. What is new is not the movement: it is choosing which place the enemy is walking toward.

Search terms for this lesson“in unity how to make an enemy chase the player, how to find the player transform, how to move an enemy toward a target”Solo build
Break It Down~10 minSolo build

An enemy that comes for me when I get close. That is the whole feature, and like every feature in this course it is not one problem — it is several standing in a line, one of which you have never solved before.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

No parts listed here on purpose. Splitting the problem up is the work of this lesson — write your list before you open the file.

Most of the parts inside this feature are things you have already built somewhere else: a trigger and a bool from the turret, a movement toward a target from the guard. Only one part has no earlier version — deciding which place the enemy is walking toward, and guaranteeing that exactly one movement line runs. That is what a well-sequenced course feels like from the inside: the same parts in a new order, with one genuinely new one among them.

The test for a finished split: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the enemy chase me" cannot be looked up. "Do something different while the player is inside a trigger" can. If a part is still too big to search for, it is two parts.

Your turn

List the parts of this problem, in the order you would build them.

The enemy never gets a second movement line — it gets a second destination. Name the one variable both behaviours write, and say what the player would see if you added a separate chase movement instead.

In the Editor ~15 min
  1. Scene view → save the Overworld before you touch anything, then Project window → Assets/Prefabs/MobileEnemy. All four instances share one prefab, so a change to the radius changes all four — but the radius is a collider, so an instance can override it. Decide before you write anything.
  2. Hierarchy → MobileEnemy → Detection Radius: a Circle Collider 2D with Is Trigger ticked and Radius 5. That is the aggro radius — a shape the player can see in the Scene view, not a number buried in a script.
  3. Inspector → the prefab root: the EnemyController from 4.1, with its Capsule Collider 2D and Dynamic Rigidbody 2D. The body is already there; today's code still moves the Transform, and the note at the bottom of the code half says what that costs.
  4. Game view → press Play and walk near an enemy with the Console open. It ignores you and walks its beat. That is the "before" you are about to change.
  5. Once the code half is done — Play again and cross the ring slowly. Watch where the change of direction happens relative to the circle you can see in the Scene view: it is the collider, not a distance the enemy measured.
In the Code ~30 min

No API table: every call today is one you have already made. One file — Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs, your patrol from 4.1.

Slow down on one part: choosing the destination. Every target you have moved toward so far was placed in the scene — a patrol point you wired in 4.1. This time the same movement line has two possible destinations, and a remembered answer decides which one it gets. That is where the bugs will be: not in the arithmetic, but in which branch ran.

The one fact I will hand you: Vector3.MoveTowards(transform.position, targetPosition, step) already works out the direction from the two positions, every frame. You do not need a subtraction, a .normalized or a velocity — the 4.1 line is the whole chase as long as targetPosition is right.

The second decision is not about maths. Your Update() patrols unconditionally and now has to chase as well — two behaviours that want the same object, with no earlier lesson to copy from. Pick one of these three on purpose:

How the two behaviours coexistWhat the code does each frameWhat the player seesThe risk
Chase is an if; patrol is the else — this project The branch picks a destination; then the one movement line runs, wherever the destination came from. A clean switch: the moment you cross the line, the enemy stops walking its beat and comes for you. Exactly one writer moves the enemy, so nothing fights — but the branch has to be written in the right order, and the patrol's own index is frozen while the chase runs, not reset.
Chase is an if; the patrol keeps running anyway Both call a movement in the same frame, each with its own destination. A stutter, or an enemy that drifts toward you while still dutifully stepping through its route. Two systems moving one object, and their sum is a third movement nobody designed. With the 4.1 route this is easy to miss: the patrol's arrival check still fires, so the index advances underneath the chase and the beat restarts somewhere new.
Chase is an if; the patrol is switched off by a flag The flag records the mode, and the patrol checks it. Same as the first row, at first. One extra field, and one extra thing to keep true — and the moment you have a third behaviour, one more clause in every check. Keep this thought: the Enemy State Machines reference is where it goes next.
Architectural specification for the chase.
  • Which two fields does the trigger write, and which one has to start false? What does target hold — the player's collider, the player's GameObject, or the player's Transform — and which of those does the destination line need?
  • What happens on the way out of the circle, and why does the exit callback set target = null rather than leave the old reference lying around? Name the exception the other choice leaves behind.
  • Which branch wins when the enemy is inside its patrol beat and inside the aggro radius at the same time? Point at the line that decides it.
  • Does the patrol's own memory — its index — reset or freeze while the chase runs? Say what the player sees either way.
  • What does the enemy do while chasing that a wall should stop, and what actually stops it? The body is Dynamic and the movement is a Transform write — say what that means in one sentence.

Socratic: States, Transitions and Two Writers

  1. You gave the turret a trigger in 3.1 and it opened fire. What does the enemy do with that same answer that the turret did not do — and why does that make the enemy harder to build?
  2. Your enemy is inside its patrol beat and inside the aggro radius at the same time. Which behaviour must win? Describe exactly what the player sees if you pick the other one.
  3. If both behaviours moved the enemy in one frame, what is the sum of "walk right at 2 units per second" and "walk toward the player at 2 units per second"? Why is that sum not a chase — and how does one shared destination avoid it?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break the chase into parts, and say in one line what each part does and where you built it before
  • Explain why the aggro radius is a collider rather than a number in the script, and what the trigger needs in order to fire at all
  • Explain your patrol-to-chase transition, point at the construct that stops both behaviours running at once, and say why two writers on one transform produce motion nobody designed
  • Say what target holds, what happens to it on exit, and why null is the right value there
  • Design an aggro radius that reads as fair next to the turret's detection range, and say which of the two the player should meet first
  • Commit and push
